title: Boots's Dixieland drumming and Fats Martin
summary: The 1929 State Fair band had a New Orleans beat; Fats Martin set the tempos.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: I was listening to Boots' Callous Love. And he even got sort of a Dixieland sound.
Boots was, to me, a Dixieland drummer.
Yeah. The only thing, he wasn't from New Orleans. Yeah. The guy had a real Dixieland beat. Good beat. Good drummer. Good cymbal man.
Yeah, I was impressed with that, that a guy would have that kind of Dixieland flavor to his plan.
That's right. Yeah, some good musicians in the band, I feel, they could easily sit in the Dixieland band and play it.
Whereas your band, unless I knew you were from New Orleans, I would not necessarily have spotted it, maybe Contrell, you know, because you didn't, on the record I'm talking about, you know.

Yeah, that wasn't later, that's after the big arrangements came up. Yes. But at the first plane, which we don't have any records of, in 1929 at the State Fair, nine musicians from New Orleans, you didn't have anything but a New Orleans beat. Yeah. Everybody was from New Orleans, except for one man, Hiram Hardy.
But those records are not captured in those days. Yeah, all that stuff. The ones that are captured now, in the later years, when the arrangements and the style of the band had changed.
You had to change the style of the band, yeah. Yeah.

But there was always that, they said, there's something about this band that makes you want to dance. Well, I've got to give credit to Fats Martin. Now, if you close the curtain in front of Freddie Coleman, and close your eyes, you'd hear Fats Martin. It's almost identical. Fats Martin was the greatest drumming that I've ever heard. And he set the tempos. And it was something, now and then a fast number, which people would try to dance on, but they couldn't. It was mostly a feature number that featured musicians.
